Studies of reproductive biology in the Orange-eared tanager (Chlorochrysa calliparaea) indicate that females typically produce a single clutch each year [F_R_i = a single clutch each year], containing two eggs [N_R_i = containing two eggs], a modest annual reproductive output that aligns with patterns observed in other small-bodied neotropical frugivores. When maintained under controlled conditions at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], representing the species' active metabolic phase, the interval between successive breeding attempts is constrained by a protracted period of parental care and resource acquisition. The available data on net reproductive rate are derived from these two component measurements, which together describe the species' conservative life history strategy. This slow pace of reproduction is characteristic of many tanagers inhabiting stable tropical environments where adult survival is prioritized over high fecundity. The clutch size is small relative to temperate passerines, reflecting energetic limitations tied to fruit availability and the demands of extended brooding periods. Fully grown adults attain an ultimate wet weight of approximately 21.5 grams [Wwi = approximately 21.5 grams].

Neonatal body mass has been recorded in field studies of closely related species to provide estimates for this genus. Hatchlings of the Orange-eared tanager emerge at a wet weight of approximately 2.9 grams [Wwb = approximately 2.9 grams], a value that is comparable to that documented for the congeneric Chlorochrysa nitidissima. This initial mass represents a substantial energetic investment from the female, given that the calcareous egg constitutes a significant proportion of her body size prior to laying. The altricial nestlings are entirely dependent on biparental provisioning during the early postnatal period, and their low birth mass necessitates rapid growth to reach independence. In comparison to other Thraupidae of similar adult dimensions, the neonatal mass of approximately 2.9 grams [Wwb = approximately 2.9 grams] is consistent with a life history strategy emphasizing high-quality parental care rather than large initial offspring size. This early stage is critical, as mortality risks are elevated before the chicks achieve thermal independence.

Field observations and captive rearing experiments have clarified the developmental timeline of this species. Eggs incubated at a constant temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C] exhibit an incubation period of roughly 17 days [ab = roughly 17 days], a duration that is consistent with data reported for C. nitidissima. The incubation stage is followed by a nestling phase during which the chicks are brooded extensively by the female while the male provisions both the female and the offspring. The age at hatching is relatively short compared to some larger tanager species, likely due to the moderate egg size and the high ambient temperatures that accelerate embryonic development within the nest environment. Once hatched, the growing chicks experience a rapid increase in body mass, transitioning from their initial 2.9 grams [Wwb = 2.9 grams] to a substantially heavier fledgling mass over the course of the nestling period. The thermal conditions of 36 °C [T = 36 °C] during incubation appear critical for normal development, as deviations can lead to extended incubation times or reduced hatching success.

Under the sustained thermal conditions characteristic of the species' active metabolism, measured at an ambient temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], several key life history transitions have been documented. Fledging, defined as the first achievement of sustained flight and departure from the nest, occurs at 21 days after hatching [tx = 21 days after hatching] at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This developmental milestone is followed by a period of post-fledging dependence during which the young continue to be fed by the parents while they refine their foraging skills. Sexual maturity, or puberty, is attained considerably later, with gonadal maturation completed by 63 days after hatching [tp = 63 days after hatching] at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This extended interval between fledging and reproductive maturity allows the juvenile to develop the flight musculature and cognitive abilities necessary for independent survival in the forest canopy. In the context of tropical passerines, an age at maturity of 63 days after hatching [tp = 63 days after hatching] is relatively rapid, enabling individuals to contribute to the next breeding season within the same calendar year under favorable conditions at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C].

Long-term demographic monitoring of banded populations has provided estimates of maximum longevity and first reproduction. At the stable body temperature associated with active foraging and breeding (41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]), the maximum lifespan for the Orange-eared tanager is approximately 9 years [am = approximately 9 years]. This relatively high adult survival is typical of tropical avian species that experience low extrinsic mortality rates. The age at first successful brood, measured as the time from the individual's own birth to the production of its first clutch of two eggs, is 365 days since birth [tR = 365 days since birth] at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This indicates that most individuals breed for the first time at the beginning of their second calendar year, following the completion of juvenile molting and territory establishment. Given the species' annual clutch frequency of merely a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], each breeding attempt carries heightened importance for lifetime reproductive success, particularly as the long lifespan (9 years) [am = 9 years] provides multiple opportunities to replace failed nests or exploit favorable conditions at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C].
